title: Inflation (up) news: Diesel bets surge as hedge funds turn most bullish on oil since May
body: While crude positioning has grabbed headlines, the sharper move is in refined products, and that matters more directly for inflation than the Brent number alone. Diesel feeds almost every stage of the physical economy, freight, agriculture, construction and shipping, so a sustained rally at the pump flows through to broader costs faster than a crude price move does. Record US retail diesel prices alongside the highest net-bullish diesel positioning since March point to a market pricing in prolonged tightness rather than a temporary spike. With gasoline bets also at their most bullish seasonal level on record, the combined refined products picture suggests headline inflation pressure from energy is building even before any further escalation around Hormuz. --- Last week (don't miss this information): Diesel crunch, hot ISM data point to entrenched inflation risk: gold, equity risks --- Crude positioning has hit a three-month high, but it is the sharper rally in diesel and gasoline, and the inflation risk that comes with it, that stands out most this week.

title: Yen's sharp weekly rally tied to BOJ rate hike repricing
body: The move in USD/JPY, from near 160 to under156 over the space of a week, reflects a rapid repricing of BOJ intentions rather than a broader dollar story, with markets now treating a September hike as close to fully priced. The more consequential swing factor is the roughly one-in-four probability now attached to a second, back-to-back hike as soon as October, since that scenario would mark a genuine departure from the BOJ's historic six-month cadence between moves. A faster BOJ tightening path also carries flow-on effects for yen crosses more broadly, including AUD/JPY, where a narrowing rate differential and unwind of yen-funded carry positions could add downside pressure on the cross if the hawkish repricing continues. --- The yen just had its best week in a month, and it's the market's growing belief in back-to-back BOJ hikes, not just one hike, driving the move.

title: Hormuz traffic sinks to lowest since May, despite US Navy's escort claims
body: The gap between the Navy's account and the independent traffic data is itself the market-relevant signal. Kpler's 10-day average of just 10 vessels a day, the lowest since May, points to genuine physical tightness in Hormuz-transiting supply regardless of how safe passage is being characterised publicly, keeping the geopolitical risk premium in oil firmly intact. With Marisks assessing risk as extreme for Iranian-linked tonnage and materially elevated for US-linked shipping, insurance and freight costs for any vessel attempting the route are likely to stay elevated, reinforcing upward pressure on landed crude costs even before accounting for the direct loss of throughput. The fact that a refined products tanker was turned back attempting to exit adds a further squeeze on product availability layered on top of the crude disruption. -- Independent shipping data show Hormuz traffic at its lowest since May, a picture that sits awkwardly next to the US Navy's own account of stepped-up tanker escorts.

title: Goldman says inflation data, not jobs, will decide Fed's September call
body: Goldman's view pushes back against a simple read-through from August's jobs strength to a September hike, framing next week's CPI print as the real swing factor for the Fed decision. If Goldman's benign inflation call proves right, that argues against the further upside in short-term US rates that stronger jobs data alone might suggest, a dynamic with direct implications for the US dollar and, by extension, AUD/USD. Goldman's framing of the current inflation overshoot as driven by fading special factors, tariffs, energy prices and nonmarket costs, also matters for how durable any near-term inflation surprise is judged to be, shaping how much weight markets place on a single CPI print heading into the meeting. --- Goldman Sachs says the jobs data clears one hurdle to a Fed hike in September, but it's next week's inflation print, not payrolls, that will actually decide the outcome.

title: ICYMI: Fed's Hammack says "its time to act" to cool inflation
body: Hammack's comments add another hawkish voice to a Fed that already looks more split than usual heading into the 15 to 16 September meeting, reinforcing a market that has moved to price slightly above 60 percent odds of a rate increase following Friday's strong jobs report. Her framing, that policy is not sufficiently restrictive rather than merely on hold, keeps upside risk in play for short-term rates and the dollar into the blackout period. With Hammack among three dissenters from July's hold decision, her remarks read less as new information and more as a data point confirming how quickly sentiment has shifted since the jobs report landed. --- Greg had this Friday: Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack is sounding decidedly hawkish on monetary policy ---- In case you missed it from Friday, Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack said the time has come to act on inflation, just as a strong jobs report pushed rate hike odds above 60 percent.

title: Japan Forex Reserves Hit Nearly 4-Year Low
body: Japan's foreign exchange reserves declined by USD 79.58 billion in August 2026 to USD 1.208 trillion, down from USD 1.287 trillion in July, reaching their lowest level since October 2022. Foreign currency reserves totaled USD 994.98 billion, comprising USD 839.56 billion in securities and USD 155.42 billion in deposits. Of these deposits, USD 154.98 billion were held with foreign central banks and the Bank for International Settlements (BIS). Deposits with banks headquartered in Japan amounted to USD 409 million, while those with banks headquartered outside Japan came to USD 25 million. Japan's reserve position at the IMF was USD 11.42 billion, and its holdings of Special Drawing Rights (SDRs) were valued at USD 61.17 billion. Gold reserves stood at USD 124.10 billion. title: Japan's Foreign Reserves Drop to $1.21 Trillion in August, Marking Notable Monthly Decline
body: Japan's foreign exchange reserves fell in August 2026, slipping to USD 1,207.5 billion from USD 1,287.1 billion in July 2026, according to data updated on 6 September 2026. The move represents a noticeable month-on-month decline in the country's reserve stockpile. The contraction in reserves comes after Japan had maintained a higher level of foreign assets in July, suggesting a shift in reserve dynamics over the summer period. While the data release does not specify the underlying drivers, changes of this scale are often associated with valuation effects from currency movements, shifts in global bond prices, or potential market operations. With foreign reserves a key buffer for external stability and a signal watched closely by global investors, the August reading will likely draw attention from market participants tracking Japan's capacity to manage currency volatility and external shocks in the months ahead. title: Oil Rises as US and Iran Exchange Fire
body: Crude oil climbed above $92 per barrel on Monday, extending last week's gains as the US and Iran traded strikes in the Middle East, heightening fears of prolonged disruptions to regional energy supplies. Over the weekend, the US targeted three Iranian oil tankers in retaliation for ballistic missile attacks on US Navy warships. In response, Tehran announced plans to establish a new restricted zone outside the Strait of Hormuz, encompassing a US Navy blockade line and extending into parts of the Persian Gulf. At the same time, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Washington would maintain its naval presence in the Middle East, including the blockade aimed at curbing Iranian oil exports and ensuring the safe passage of commercial vessels through Hormuz. Hostilities between the two sides resumed last week after roughly a month of relative calm, driving oil prices about 10% higher as markets reassessed geopolitical and supply risks. title: NZX 50 Trades Slightly Lower to Start the Week
body: New Zealand shares slipped 21 points, or 0.2%, to 13,954 in Monday morning trade, giving back some of the prior session's gains. The move followed Friday's decline on Wall Street, as stronger-than-expected US labor data reinforced expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at its upcoming meeting. Sentiment was also restrained ahead of key Chinese data due later this week, including CPI, PPI, and August trade figures. Investors continued to track developments in the Middle East conflict after Tehran said it had targeted oil tankers in retaliation for US strikes. Domestically, traders digested Friday's comments from RBNZ Assistant Governor Karen Silk, which suggested the central bank is more likely to wait until December before implementing another rate hike. Sector-wise, technology, consumer discretionary, energy, and financial stocks exerted the most pressure on the index. Notable early decliners included Ryman Healthcare (-1.0%), ANZ Group (-0.8%), Infratil (-0.8%), and Channel Infrastructure (-0.6%).
